content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato is a nutrient‑dense root vegetable with a mild, naturally sweet flavor and soft texture when cooked, making it an ideal first food for babies from about 6 months old.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, which the body converts to vitamin A.
They are grown in tropical and subtropical regions but are available year‑round.
The sweet taste encourages infants to accept solid foods more easily.
Sweet potatoes can be served as puree, baked sticks, or soft cubes for teething.
Compared with regular potatoes, sweet potatoes have a lower glycemic index.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and cell growth.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C aids immune development and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber helps regulate digestion and prevents constipation in infants.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports electrolyte balance and heart health.

items.title: Low allergen potential
items.content: Sweet potatoes are rarely allergenic, making them a safe first vegetable.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Large pieces can pose a choking risk for babies under 12 months – offer as smooth puree or finely diced.

items.title: Potential sugar load
items.content: Because sweet potatoes are naturally sweet, serve in moderation to avoid rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Allergic reaction
items.content: Rare, but individual intolerance is possible – introduce a small amount and watch for symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam, boil, or bake the sweet potato until tender, then mash into a smooth puree. For older infants (9+ months) you can offer small soft cubes or baked sticks without added salt or sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sweet potatoes in a cool, dry place (10‑15 °C) in paper bags. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer and use within 2‑3 weeks. Avoid plastic bags to prevent moisture buildup.
